Introduction

Definition

Simulation is the imitation of the operation of a real-world process or system over time.

The act of simulating something first requires that a model be developed; this model represents the key characteristics or behaviours/functions of the selected physical or abstract system or process.

- Wikipedia.org

Games as Simulations

  • Games, on a fundamental level, are a type of simulation.
  • They take the form of an engaging rendition or combinations of real-life environments.
  • Real-life environments present familiarity to a player, and therefore work well to immerse a player.
  • Simulation Games are a specific genre of game where the game focus is the 'simulation' aspect.
  • Not all simulations are games, and not all games are 'simulation games'. But all games can be considered simulations through various aspects.

Simulation in Research vs in Games

  • The purpose of simulations in research is to accurately depict real-world scenarios in a more efficient/cheaper way.
    • Examples may include COVID spread simulations or weather simulations.
  • Within simulation games, however, accuracy can be sacrificed in favour of elements such as fantasy/entertainment.
    • The purpose of simulation games is to entertain the player as opposed to maximising realism.

Games as Real-World Simulations

  • There have been reports of football associations scouting players via FIFA.
  • A tough trade-off must be made between realism and entertainment when designing simulation games.
  • This means that game simulators cannot always be trusted to provide real-world results.
  • In the majority of cases, simulation games are tailored to be realistic to the player and less representative of the real world.

Basic Simulation Concepts

Elements or patterns that exist in the real world are often mapped mathematically and these elements can be used as tools to build a simulated game environment.

Simple Functions

  • Wave functions can work well for price fluctuations over time.
  • This can add a level of depth to games such as RPG games, where a simple wave function is used to determine e.g. the price of food on a given day.
  • Another example could be exponential curves, which are used in Pokémon games to determine the experience needed to level up.

Random Walk

  • Used extensively in game AI.
  • Creates a complicated, unpredictable pattern that can be used to create non-deterministic paths or outcomes

Particles & Meshes

Particles

  • Particle simulations will represent the objects being simulated as individual points.
  • Rules, lore and random effects can then be added to each particle in the system.
  • Particles can work well for gravity, explosions, gases, and some types of fluids.
  • They are especially good for fast-moving simulations such as explosions

Meshes

  • Mesh simulations represent objects via connected edges and vertices.
  • Unlike particles, it is very easy to deform a mesh which can be useful for certain objects.
  • Mesh simulations are slower than particles, but depict objects in a greater detail/depth.
  • Meshes work well for shapes, solids and some other kinds of fluids.

Particles and meshes can be combined into one simulation, although it is useful to split them conceptually into different aspects.

Time-Stepping: Simulating Over Time

  • Time-based simulations will require a clock implementation within the code.
  • Time will be advanced step-by-step.
  • We can define the time-step and the number of iterations ourselves.

x = OurSimulation() # Define our simulation, whatever we are doing
t_end = 10.0 # Time value to stop the simulation

while t < t_end:
	x.evolve(duration=1) # This is doing the simulation step, whatever it may be
	t = t + 1

t will begin at a value of 0. By the end of our while loop, t will have a value of 9. This represents 10 timesteps of one second (i.e. 10 seconds) of simulation running time.

  • If a simulation is too long it may not provide results of value (e.g. results may repeat) or become too costly to run.
  • However, if a simulation is not long enough, there also may not be enough time to see results of value.

Simulating Physics: Examples

Moving Ball Example

  • Imagine we are simulating a moving ball in a 2D plane.
  • We want to ensure we are modelling both the x and y values of the ball position.

To start with, we will model the ball so that it has an x-velocity of 10.0 and a y-velocity of 0 (i.e. it is stationary).

# Define our starting values
t = 0 # seconds
t_end = 10.0 # seconds
x = 0 # Starting XPos
y = 10 # Starting YPos

vx = 10 # Define Velocity-X, m/s
vy = 0 # Define Velocity-Y, m/s

while t < t_end:
	# The code on this indent level represents one time-step.
	print(t,x,y)
	x = x + 1 * vx
	y = y + 1 * vy
	t = t + 1

Output Values (t,x,y)

0, 0, 10

1, 10, 10

2, 20, 10

3, 30, 10

4, 40, 10

...

Modifications

  • Changing the vx value will result in the ball moving a greater distance per time-step.
  • Changing the t + 1 increment will alter how often the ball will actually be shown to move.
    • Here it is once per second but a value like t = t + 0.1 will show the ball moving ten times per second
  • Changing the t_end value will change how long our simulation actually runs for overall.

Adding Air Resistance

We can add an air resistance/drag coefficient to make our simulation more realistic.

# Define our starting values
t = 0 # seconds
t_end = 10.0 # seconds
x = 0 # Starting XPos
y = 10 # Starting YPos

# Now we are adding an air resistance value...
air_drag_coefficient = 0.1 # (m/s^2 ---> This is an acceleration!)

vx = 10 # Define Velocity-X, m/s
vy = 0 # Define Velocity-Y, m/s

while t < t_end:
	# The code on this indent level represents one time-step.
	print(t,x,y)
	x = x + 1 * vx
	y = y + 1 * vy
	t = t + 1
	# We want to reduce our vx for each time-step...
	vx = vx * (1.0 - air_drag_coefficient)

The above code will make our ball slow down by 10% of the previous value each time, in the x-direction, for each time-step.

Output Values (t,x,y)

0, 0, 10

1, 10, 10

2, 19, 10

3, 27.9, 10

4, 34.4, 10

...

Adding Gravity

  • For realistic gravity, we can use the gravitational constant .
  • On earth, the value of is 
# Define our starting values
t = 0 # seconds
t_end = 10.0 # seconds
x = 0 # Starting XPos
y = 10 # Starting YPos

vx = 10 # Define Velocity-X, m/s
vy = 0 # Define Velocity-Y, m/s

while t < t_end:
	# The code on this indent level represents one time-step.
	print(t,x,y)
	x = x + 1 * vx
	y = y + 1 * vy
	t = t + 1
	# We'll add in this line below to reduce the Y velocity
	vy -= 9.81
  • For our simulated gravity, we want to reduce (i.e. -9.81) the y-velocity by this factor for each time-step.
    • We are reducing because we want our ball to move downwards in the -Y direction.

Output Values (t,x,y)

0, 0, 10

1, 10, 10

2, 19, 0.19

3, 27.9, -19.43

4, 34.4, -48.86

...

As shown in the output, it is apparent that for each time-step, our ball is now moving downwards at an increasing velocity (as if it's moving through gravity).

  • Changing this 9.81 value to something lower can be useful in games where we want to simulate an environment with lower gravity, such as the moon.
